strengths: The paper provides a careful empirical analysis of cross-attention distributions across verbatim vs. template memorization and across two SD architectures, revealing that the prior state-of-the-art's EOT/padding-only attenuation strategy (Ren et al., 2024) is insufficient for verbatim memorization (other tokens spike higher) and actively counterproductive for template memorization (EOT attention is not elevated, sometimes lower, for memorized examples). This analysis is a genuine and useful contribution beyond just proposing a new algorithm.

The proposed GUARD framework is a clean and intuitive generalization of classifier-free guidance that adds both a repulsion term (away from the standard/memorized conditional prediction) and an attraction term (toward a safer positive target), addressing the common failure mode where pure repulsion causes fidelity collapse.

The dynamic, per-prompt, per-step statistical spike detector (Z-score based) for locating memorization-critical token positions is a sensible, well-motivated design that removes the need for hard-coded token categories (EOT/padding/BOT), and the ablations (Sections A.5-A.7) systematically justify design choices (which blocks, which heads, which timesteps).

Evaluation is comprehensive: two architectures, two memorization types, multiple metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID), several strong recent baselines, both a stricter filtered protocol and the traditional Pareto-frontier protocol used by prior work, plus efficiency and robustness-to-non-memorized-prompts analyses.

The paper is transparent about an important methodological critique of prior evaluation practice (including low-memorization examples inflates apparent success), and its proposed filtering (SSCD > 0.7) is a valuable, reproducible improvement in evaluation rigor that other work in the area should adopt.
Reasonably honest limitations/impact section acknowledging that inference-time methods do not remove memorized information from the weights and remain vulnerable to white-box extraction.
weaknesses: Hyperparameters (α, τ, and r for GUARD) are tuned separately per architecture/memorization-type setting via grid search (Table 2), and it is unclear how these would be selected in a deployment setting where a practitioner does not know a priori whether a given prompt is verbatim- or template-memorized (or memorized at all). No automatic hyperparameter selection or single global default is demonstrated across settings, which raises concerns about real-world applicability despite the appendix showing default CA attenuation hyperparameters are at least harmless on non-memorized prompts.

The core algorithmic novelty relative to Ren et al. (2024) is somewhat incremental: both approaches attenuate cross-attention logits at trigger-token positions before softmax; the main difference is dynamic per-prompt outlier detection instead of fixed EOT/padding targeting. While well justified empirically, this narrows the claimed originality of the 'instantiation' contribution (as opposed to the GUARD framework itself, which is more novel).

Quality evaluation relies solely on automated proxies (CLIP score, FID); no human perceptual study is conducted to confirm that 'high-quality' images are actually preserved from a human standpoint, which is important given that the abstract explicitly claims the method does not hurt image generation quality.

Experiments are limited to older/smaller SD v1.4 and v2.0 U-Net architectures; there is no evaluation on more modern text-to-image backbones (e.g., SDXL, DiT/transformer-based diffusion models), limiting confidence that findings (e.g., block/head localization patterns) generalize to current architectures.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are based on only 4 generations per prompt, and while 95% CIs are reported for SSCD/CLIP, no paired significance testing across methods is presented; some CLIP/FID differences between CA-in-GUARD and baselines appear to fall within overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Table 1, SD v1.4 verbatim CLIP), yet the paper repeatedly claims to be 'by far' superior across metrics.

The method requires effectively 3 conditional forward passes per denoising step (unconditional, memorized-conditional, spike-attenuated-conditional) plus per-step spike recomputation, and although batching mitigates this, Table 5 shows CA-in-GUARD is roughly 1.4-2x slower than no-mitigation/CA-attenuation-only, which is a non-trivial overhead not deeply analyzed for scalability to production settings.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely useful empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns (Figure 1) showing that EOT-only attenuation (the prior SOTA mechanism of Ren et al.) is insufficient for verbatim memorization (other tokens spike higher) and can be actively counterproductive for template memorization (EOT attention is actually lower for memorized vs non-memorized prompts in early steps). This is a clear, well-motivated finding that explains why prior work fails to generalize across memorization types.

The GUARD framework is a reasonably clean generalization of classifier-free guidance with separate attraction/repulsion terms, and the paper is careful to separate the contribution of the general framework from the specific CA-attenuation instantiation.

Broad and systematic ablations are provided in the appendix (U-Net blocks, attention heads, timesteps, alternative semantic targets, robustness on non-memorized prompts, computational cost), which supports reproducibility and gives insight into design choices.
Evaluation spans two architectures and both verbatim and template memorization, exposing that no single prior baseline is consistently best across settings -- a useful observation for the field.

The paper is transparent about the non-standard filtering/evaluation protocol it adopts and explains its rationale, and also reports results under the traditional protocol in the appendix for comparability.
weaknesses: Claims of GUARD/CA-in-GUARD 'dominating' or being 'by far the most robust' are overstated relative to the actual numbers: in several settings (e.g., SD v2.0 template memorization in Table 1) CA-in-GUARD and the plain CA-attenuation ablation are statistically indistinguishable (identical SSCD 0.193±0.014, nearly identical CLIP), so the added repulsion machinery of GUARD contributes little in these cases despite its extra computational cost.

The method's core mechanism requires a conditional forward pass on the exact memorized prompt to obtain both the negative target and the attention maps used for spike detection, implicitly assuming the deployer already knows a prompt is memorized. This practical prerequisite (memorized-prompt identification) is not discussed as a central limitation, and the only experiment addressing non-memorized prompts (Appendix A.3) tests CA-attenuation alone, not the full GUARD pipeline with the repulsion term, leaving the realistic deployment scenario insufficiently evaluated.

No qualitative/visual examples of generated images are shown anywhere in the main paper (or appendix, from what is provided) to let a reader judge whether 'quality is not hurt,' despite quality preservation being a central claim; the evaluation relies entirely on automated proxy metrics (CLIP, FID, SSCD).

The custom evaluation protocol (filtering to SSCD>0.7, custom 15% CLIP-degradation thresholds for 'best' hyperparameter selection per method) is a substantial departure from prior work's protocol, and while motivated, it makes the reported baseline numbers not directly comparable to the original papers; combined with per-method, per-setting grid search, there is a risk of unequal tuning effort or protocol choices implicitly favoring the proposed method.

GUARD incurs a non-trivial computational overhead (roughly 1.3-1.5x wall-clock runtime over no-mitigation and over the authors' own CA-attenuation-only variant per Table 5), which is a meaningful cost for an approach whose main selling point is inference-time efficiency relative to training-/finetuning-time alternatives.

The 'novel statistical mechanism' for spike detection is a simple Z-score outlier threshold (with threshold τ as a tuned hyperparameter per setting), which is a fairly standard technique; framing it as a significant methodological novelty somewhat overstates its originality.

Comparisons against very recent (2025) concurrent baselines (e.g., Han et al., posted around the same time as this submission) raise questions about whether those baselines were adequately tuned/reproduced versus the authors' own extensively tuned method.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem (memorization mitigation in T2I diffusion models) with a clean conceptual framing that extends classifier-free guidance with both attraction and repulsion terms (GUARD).

The empirical analysis of cross-attention distributions across verbatim vs. template memorization (Figure 1) is a genuine and useful contribution, convincingly showing that prior EOT-only attenuation strategies (Ren et al.) are mis-specified for template memorization, which is a novel and well-supported finding.

The proposed per-prompt, on-the-fly statistical spike detector is a reasonable and relatively simple mechanism that avoids hard-coded token categories used in prior work, and the ablations (blocks, heads, timesteps, alternative attract targets) are thorough and help justify design choices.

Evaluation spans two architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0) and both memorization types, with a more rigorous protocol than prior work (filtering low-SSCD examples, separate reporting by memorization type, hyperparameter selection tied to acceptable quality degradation), which makes the comparison more informative than typical single-operating-point comparisons.

Includes a sanity check on non-memorized prompts (Appendix A.3) showing the method does not require a priori knowledge of which prompts are memorized and does not harm quality on non-memorized inputs, which strengthens practical applicability.

Reasonably comprehensive baseline comparison (RTA, Wen et al., Ren et al., Han et al.) and consideration of multiple trade-off axes (best-SSCD, best-CLIP, best-FID) rather than a single cherry-picked configuration.
weaknesses: Results are not uniformly state-of-the-art: e.g., in Table 1 (SD v2.0, template memorization) both CA attenuation and CA-in-GUARD have noticeably worse FID (245.9 and 212.7) than Wen et al. (188.9), undercutting the claim that the method 'improves upon or yields comparable results' in quality; similarly CA-in-GUARD's SSCD on SD v2.0 is identical to plain CA attenuation (0.193 both), suggesting the attraction/repulsion mechanism contributes little in that setting despite the paper's narrative of synergy.

The hyperparameter search ranges for τ and α differ drastically across settings (e.g., τ in [0.01,0.05] for verbatim vs. [0.5,3.0] for template memorization; Table 2), indicating the method requires substantial per-setting/per-architecture retuning rather than being a truly 'automatic' or universal detector, which weakens the 'surgical' and 'dynamic' framing and raises reproducibility/generalization concerns for new models or datasets not covered by the grid search.

Evaluation is restricted to older SD v1.4/v2.0 U-Net architectures; no experiments on more modern architectures (e.g., SDXL, DiT/transformer-based diffusion backbones) that are increasingly standard, limiting the evidence for general applicability of the cross-attention-based mechanism.

The method requires three (batched) U-Net passes per step and a full per-step CA extraction/spike-detection computation; wall-clock numbers (Table 5) show CA-in-GUARD is roughly 1.4-1.7x slower than no-mitigation/CA-attenuation and comparable to or only modestly faster than the costliest baselines (Han et al., Ren et al.), somewhat undercutting the 'minimal impact to efficiency' claim made in the introduction.

Quality is assessed only via automated proxies (CLIP score, FID); no human evaluation of perceptual quality or semantic alignment is reported, which is a common but non-trivial limitation given that FID/CLIP can be insensitive to subtle quality degradations introduced by attention manipulation.

The threshold-based outlier detection (Z>τ) and multiplicative logit attenuation are reasonable but fairly simple heuristics with limited theoretical grounding for why they constitute a good 'positive target' beyond the empirical comparison against one alternative (semantic paraphrase) in the ablation; the mechanism's behavior under compounding/multiple spikes per prompt or very short/long prompts is not analyzed.

The evaluation dataset (500 memorized examples from Webster, 2023, filtered to high-SSCD subsets of 72-143 prompts) is relatively small and specific to LAION-based SD models; generalization to other training corpora or newer memorization benchmarks is untested.

strengths: Thorough empirical analysis of cross-attention distributions distinguishing verbatim vs. template memorization, revealing that prior EOT-only attenuation strategies (Ren et al., 2024) are miscalibrated for template memorization — this is a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution.

The GUARD framework (attraction + repulsion contrastive guidance) is a reasonably novel reformulation of CFG for memorization mitigation, and the dynamic per-prompt statistical spike detector is a sensible, well-motivated improvement over static/hard-coded token selection.

Extensive experimentation: two/three SD architectures (v1.4, v2.0, and additionally v3.0), both memorization types, multiple baselines, and a wide array of ablations (U-Net blocks, attention heads, timesteps, samplers, CFG scales, guidance schedules).

Good supplementary validation: DINO-based retrieval metrics as an independent check on SSCD conclusions, full-spectrum evaluation beyond the filtered high-memorization subset, robustness check on non-memorized prompts, and computational efficiency comparisons.

Reasonably transparent reporting of trade-offs (best-SSCD vs best-CLIP vs best-FID configurations) rather than cherry-picking a single operating point, plus an honest limitations section acknowledging that inference-time mitigation does not remove memorized information from weights.
weaknesses: The relationship between the general GUARD 'framework' and its sole instantiation (CA-in-GUARD) is somewhat circular: the positive target is just an attenuated version of the same conditional pass, and CA attenuation alone (r=0) is presented as already state-of-the-art, which blurs how much the 'framework' contributes beyond the underlying attention-attenuation mechanism; no alternative instantiation is shown to work well (the ablation with semantic/paraphrase targets underperforms substantially).

CA attenuation alone shows a clear FID regression on SD v2.0 (245.85 vs. 208-234 for baselines in Table 1), which is only fixed once combined with the repulsion term in GUARD — this undercuts the claim that CA attenuation is a strong standalone contribution and raises questions about why the combination is needed to patch this specific weakness rather than being a genuine synergy.

The evaluation protocol (15% CLIP degradation threshold, high-memorization-only filtering at SSCD>0.7, per-metric best-configuration selection) is self-designed by the authors specifically for this paper, and while reasonable, this bespoke protocol somewhat complicates direct comparison with numbers reported in the original baseline papers; the paper does not report statistical significance tests beyond confidence intervals for the many pairwise comparisons made.

There is an internal inconsistency in the reported hyperparameter search ranges for τ (Table 2 shows τ ranges like [0.01,0.05] for one setting and [0.5,3.0]/[1.5,3.0] for others) versus the τ=3 'e.g.' value given in the main text for the Z-score threshold, which is confusing and not reconciled, raising minor reproducibility concerns.

It is unclear whether baseline methods (Ren et al., Wen et al., Han et al.) were re-implemented by the authors or run with official code/checkpoints under the authors' new protocol; given the substantial performance gaps reported (e.g., Ren et al. underperforming its own paper's claims), some risk of implementation or tuning discrepancies favoring the proposed method cannot be fully ruled out from the text alone.

The method requires three forward passes per denoising step (batched for efficiency), which adds non-trivial overhead (Table 8 shows CA-in-GUARD roughly 1.3-1.5x runtime of no-mitigation and higher than plain CA attenuation), a cost that is somewhat downplayed relative to the 'surgical'/efficient framing in the abstract and introduction.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically relevant problem (memorization mitigation in T2I diffusion models) and proposes an inference-time approach that avoids the practical drawbacks of training-time and finetuning-time interventions, which is a sensible positioning given modern pretrained-model pipelines.

The empirical analysis of cross-attention spikes across verbatim vs. template memorization (Figure 1) is a genuinely useful contribution: it convincingly shows that attenuating only the EOT token (as in Ren et al., 2024) is insufficient and can even be counter-productive for template memorization, motivating a more dynamic, per-prompt detection scheme.

The GUARD framework (attraction + repulsion added to CFG) is a reasonably clean and general formulation, and the paper shows a concrete instantiation (CA-in-GUARD) with an automatic, on-the-fly statistical spike-detection mechanism that is more principled than prior hard-coded attention redistribution rules.

The experimental scope is broad: multiple architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0, and a transformer-based v3.0), both memorization types, several metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID, DINO retrieval), and numerous ablations (U-Net blocks, attention heads, timesteps, samplers, CFG scales, non-memorized prompt robustness, computational efficiency).
The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations (Appendix A.1) and provides extensive implementation details and hyperparameter search ranges, aiding reproducibility to a degree.
weaknesses: The central claim that CA-in-GUARD is 'by far the most robust' method and 'dominates across settings' is not fully supported by the paper's own data: in Table 1 (SD v1.4, template memorization), Han et al. (2025) achieves a better (lower) SSCD (0.479) than CA-in-GUARD (0.517), directly contradicting the dominance narrative in that setting. This inconsistency between the claimed contribution and the reported numbers is concerning and is not clearly acknowledged or explained in the main text.

The evaluation protocol substantially departs from prior work (custom SSCD filtering threshold, custom CLIP degradation tolerances, per-metric 'best achievable' configurations in Figure 3). While the authors argue this is more rigorous, reporting separate 'best SSCD', 'best CLIP', and 'best FID' configurations for each method (rather than a single configuration doing well on all axes) makes it hard to assess a method's practical, deployable trade-off, and raises concerns about selective hyperparameter tuning advantaging the proposed method over baselines that may not have received equally exhaustive grid search.

The hyperparameter search ranges (Table 2) differ substantially across architecture/memorization settings (e.g., τ ranges of [0.01,0.05] vs [1.5,3.0]), indicating that the 'dynamic' and 'surgical' method still requires considerable per-setting manual tuning, somewhat undercutting the claimed practicality/automation of the approach.

No statistical significance testing is reported for comparisons between CA-in-GUARD and the strongest baselines; some differences (e.g., identical SSCD values between CA attenuation and CA-in-GUARD in SD v2.0 template memorization, 0.193 vs 0.193) suggest the repulsion term's marginal contribution may not always be meaningful.

Despite the proposed mitigation, absolute memorization levels remain high in several settings (e.g., SSCD ≈ 0.52 for SD v1.4 template memorization, ≈0.19 for SD v2.0), suggesting the method only partially solves the underlying problem even though it improves over baselines; this is somewhat at odds with the strong rhetorical framing ('surgical', 'state-of-the-art').

The method's efficiency costs (3x forward passes, Table 8 shows ~40-70% runtime overhead vs. no mitigation) are non-trivial, and although batching mitigates this, the net efficiency advantage over some baselines (e.g., Wen et al.) is marginal despite claims of being a lightweight, surgical approach.

Evaluation relies on a single curated prompt/image set (Webster, 2023) and automated metrics only (SSCD, CLIP, FID, DINO); no human evaluation of perceptual quality or semantic alignment is provided, which is a common limitation but still weakens confidence in the 'quality preservation' claims.

The SD v3.0 evaluation is based on only 39 prompts with relatively weak memorization (SSCD > 0.3 threshold, much lower than the 0.7 threshold used for v1.4/v2.0), limiting the strength of claims about generalization to transformer-based architectures.

strengths: Thorough empirical analysis of cross-attention spike behavior across verbatim and template memorization types, revealing that the prior EOT-only attenuation heuristic (Ren et al.) is insufficient and sometimes counter-productive for template memorization—this is a genuinely useful mechanistic finding that motivates the proposed dynamic, per-prompt detection method.

The GUARD framework is a clean and intuitively motivated generalization of classifier-free guidance, combining a repulsion term (away from memorized noise prediction) with an attraction term toward a safer, prompt-aligned target, and the ablation showing CA-attenuation targets outperform semantic-paraphrase targets is informative.

Extensive and careful experimental protocol: filtering out low-memorization-score examples to avoid inflated apparent performance, separating verbatim vs template memorization, reporting trade-off curves (SSCD vs CLIP vs FID) rather than cherry-picked single points, and evaluating under multiple hyperparameter-selection criteria (best SSCD, best CLIP, best FID).

Broad set of ablations (U-Net block selection, attention heads, timesteps, samplers, CFG scales, guidance schedules) and additional validations (DINO retrieval metrics, full 500-example spectrum, non-memorized prompt robustness, SD v3.0 transformer-based architecture, efficiency comparisons) substantially strengthen the credibility and generality of the claims.

Results consistently show CA-in-GUARD matching or outperforming strong, recent baselines (Wen et al. 2024, Ren et al. 2024, Han et al. 2025) across architectures and memorization types, with the paper transparently noting where it is only competitive (not dominant) on certain quality metrics rather than overstating uniform superiority.

Reasonably detailed implementation/reproducibility information (hyperparameter search ranges, batching strategy for efficient joint forward passes, hardware/compute budget) and an honest limitations section acknowledging that inference-time mitigation cannot defend against white-box weight-extraction threats.
weaknesses: The core evaluation still relies on a custom, non-standard hyperparameter-selection protocol (filtering to SSCD>0.7, allowing 15% CLIP degradation from a reference) that differs from prior work's protocol; while this is argued to be more rigorous, it also makes direct comparison to numbers reported in cited baseline papers harder, and the choice of 15% threshold and SSCD>0.7 cutoff appear somewhat ad hoc without sensitivity analysis on these specific thresholds.

FID is computed against a generic 10,000-image LAION reference set rather than per-prompt nearest neighbors or a more targeted reference distribution, which is a coarse quality/diversity proxy and may not fully capture local fidelity degradation introduced by attention attenuation.

CA-in-GUARD requires three U-Net forward passes (or one batched triple-size pass) per denoising step, plus per-step on-the-fly statistical spike detection; although the paper reports modest wall-clock/memory overhead, the method remains more complex and compute-intensive than single-pass baselines like RTA or Wen et al., and this added complexity/engineering burden (threshold τ, scaling α, repulsion r, per-block/head choices) could hinder adoption and reproducibility by other groups.

The statistical spike-detection mechanism (mean/std-based z-score thresholding with τ=3 as example) is somewhat simplistic and its sensitivity to the chosen τ across very different prompts/datasets is not deeply analyzed theoretically, only empirically tuned per setting via grid search, raising questions about how well it would generalize to unseen datasets or substantially different model architectures without re-tuning.

The SD v3.0 evaluation uses a much smaller and weaker-memorization subset (39 of 500 prompts with SSCD>0.3, a looser threshold than the main 0.7 cutoff used elsewhere), making claims of generalization to transformer-based architectures preliminary rather than fully conclusive, and Ren et al. could not even be compared on this architecture.

The paper's claim of being 'by far the most robust/consistent' method is strong language; Table 1 and Figure 3 show CA-in-GUARD does not always have the best CLIP or FID (sometimes only comparable), so the 'improves upon or yields comparable results' framing, while honestly stated, slightly tempers the strength of the headline claim and could be presented with more nuance in the abstract/intro.
